titleEn: For His steadfast love is for ever
progression: | G G | C G | Em D | G G |
intro: Twenty six verses, and the same second half in every one of them. That is not repetition for its own sake: the psalm is a call and response, one voice reading what God did and the whole room answering. Chronicles and Ezra both show crowds answering with these exact words at dedications, so the shape is documented rather than guessed. Read down the left side only and you get the argument: creation, then the exodus, then the kings east of the Jordan, then us, then bread for everything alive. The tradition calls it the Great Hallel.

stichs.en: Give thanks to the LORD, for He is good,
for His steadfast love is for ever.

verses.summary: The opening imperative is plural: nobody sings this one alone. The ground given first is that God is good, before a single deed has been named.

stichs.en: Give thanks to the God of gods,
for His steadfast love is for ever.

verses.summary: A superlative built by construction rather than by adjective. God of gods is Hebrew for the highest of a class, and the class is not thereby conceded any members.

stichs.en: Give thanks to the Lord of lords,
for His steadfast love is for ever.

verses.summary: The second superlative closes the pair and finishes the opening frame. Both titles come from the vocabulary of overlordship, the way a great king was addressed.

stichs.en: To the One who alone does great wonders,
for His steadfast love is for ever.

verses.summary: The list of deeds opens, and the first thing said about them is alone. Everything catalogued from here down has exactly one agent.

stichs.en: To the One who made the heavens with understanding,
for His steadfast love is for ever.

verses.summary: Creation by understanding, not by force or by combat. The instrument named is a mental one, which is unusual in ancient accounts of how the sky got made.

stichs.en: To the One who spread the earth out over the waters,
for His steadfast love is for ever.

glosses: to the One who spreads out
verses.summary: The verb is metalwork: hammering a sheet out thin. It shares a root with the beaten expanse of the second day in Genesis, so the earth here is worked, not spoken.

stichs.en: To the One who made great lights,
for His steadfast love is for ever.

verses.summary: The lights get a line of their own before either of them is named, exactly as they do in the creation account. The naming is held back on purpose.

stichs.en: the sun for dominion by day,
for His steadfast love is for ever.

verses.summary: The sun is named and handed a job. Rule, not divinity: the noun is the kind of authority a king delegates to an officer who can be replaced.

stichs.en: the moon and stars for dominion by night,
for His steadfast love is for ever.

verses.summary: Moon and stars share one office and one line. The word for dominion goes plural here where the sun took the singular, which is a small grammatical courtesy to the fact that there are many of them.

stichs.en: To the One who struck Egypt through their firstborn,
for His steadfast love is for ever.

verses.summary: The hinge from cosmos to history, and the grammar does not change to mark it. Making stars and striking Egypt are stated in the same form, as one continuous series.

stichs.en: and brought Israel out from among them,
for His steadfast love is for ever.

verses.summary: The exodus put as extraction rather than escape. Israel is taken out from inside Egypt, which assumes it was embedded there and not merely camped.

stichs.en: with a strong hand and an outstretched arm,
for His steadfast love is for ever.

verses.summary: A fixed formula lifted whole out of Deuteronomy, where it belongs to the standard telling of the exodus. The psalm quotes rather than invents.

stichs.en: To the One who cut the Sea of Reeds into pieces,
for His steadfast love is for ever.

verses.summary: Not parted, cut. The verb and its object noun come from dividing a carcass or a garment, so the sea is treated as material rather than as an enemy.

stichs.en: and made Israel pass through the middle of it,
for His steadfast love is for ever.

verses.summary: The crossing gets its own verse. Splitting the sea is not the deed being praised on its own; the deed is that people walked through the gap.

stichs.en: and shook Pharaoh and his army off into the Sea of Reeds,
for His steadfast love is for ever.

verses.summary: The verb is what you do to crumbs in a garment. Pharaoh is not defeated in battle here, he is shaken out, which is a deliberate reduction of his stature.

stichs.en: To the One who led His people through the wilderness,
for His steadfast love is for ever.

verses.summary: Forty years compressed into three words, and listed among the acts of love rather than as the empty gap between two of them.

stichs.en: To the One who struck down great kings,
for His steadfast love is for ever.

verses.summary: The participle returns after two finite verbs, and it takes kings as its object. The adjective great was last attached to the lights of verse 7.

stichs.en: and killed mighty kings,
for His steadfast love is for ever.

verses.summary: The parallel line escalates twice over: struck becomes killed, and great becomes mighty. Hebrew poetry usually sharpens on the second pass rather than restating.

stichs.en: Sihon king of the Amorites,
for His steadfast love is for ever.

verses.summary: The abstraction gets a name. After Pharaoh, this is the first individual opponent identified, and he belongs to a specific road east of the Jordan.

stichs.en: and Og king of Bashan,
for His steadfast love is for ever.

verses.summary: Og gets the identical treatment, one line and a title. The pair of names stands in for the whole eastern campaign without narrating any of it.

stichs.en: and gave their land as an inheritance,
for His steadfast love is for ever.

verses.summary: The point of the two battles arrives: land. The word chosen is the legal one for property that passes down a family, not the word for spoil.

stichs.en: an inheritance for Israel His servant,
for His steadfast love is for ever.

verses.summary: The line begins by repeating the last word of the one before it and then adds the recipient. Servant here is a rank in a household, not an insult.

stichs.en: Who in our low state remembered us,
for His steadfast love is for ever.

verses.summary: The pronoun switches to us and the psalm stops being history. Whoever is singing has just been written into the list, and no event is specified.

stichs.en: and tore us free from our foes,
for His steadfast love is for ever.

verses.summary: The shortest line in the psalm, two words before the refrain. Its verb is the one used for wrenching a yoke off a neck, so the rescue is described as force applied to a fastening.

stichs.en: Who gives bread to all flesh,
for His steadfast love is for ever.

verses.summary: The widest line in the psalm, and it comes last. All flesh takes in the nations and the animals, immediately after twenty verses about one people.

stichs.en: Give thanks to the God of heaven,
for His steadfast love is for ever.

verses.summary: The closing imperative matches the three that opened the psalm, with a title that appears mainly in the latest books of the Bible. The frame shuts.

pardes.body: Every verse is cut in two by the same second half, which makes this a call and response rather than a poem read straight through: one voice takes the left side, the room answers the right. Chronicles and Ezra both record crowds answering with these exact words at dedications, so the form is attested and not merely inferred from the layout. The left side moves in three blocks. Verses 4 to 9 are creation, following the order of the first chapter of Genesis. Verses 10 to 22 are the exodus and the march east of the Jordan, ending in land held as inheritance. Verses 23 to 25 drop the past tense of history and speak as us, and the last of the three widens past Israel to everything that eats. Verses 1 to 3 and verse 26 are the frame, four calls to give thanks.

The familiar English, His mercy endures for ever, is weaker than what stands there. The noun at {{1.6}} is covenant loyalty, what one party owes another because of a bond already in place, and for ever is a stretch of time rather than a condition outside it. The grammar makes the psalm's main claim by itself: the deeds are introduced by participles, to the One who makes, to the One who spreads out at {{6.0}}, to the One who strikes, so that flattening the earth and striking Egypt are the same kind of act stated in the same shape. Lines that continue a previous one drop the participle and take a plain past verb, which is how you can tell the list's joints. Two verbs repay attention: {{15.0}}, used of shaking crumbs from a garment, and {{24.0}}, used of tearing a yoke off a neck. And the sun receives a singular dominion at {{8.2}} where the moon and stars share a plural at {{9.3}}.

The tradition calls this psalm the Great Hallel, and the reason usually given for the name is its last deed, {{25.0}}, that God gives bread to all flesh. On that reading the greatness is not the sea or the kings but the feeding of every living thing every day, and the psalm is arranged as a descent from the spectacular to the ordinary with the ordinary as the climax. The count of verses, twenty six, matches the numerical value of the four letter divine name, and the match is widely taken as deliberate rather than accidental. The turn at {{23.0}} is where the reciters stop being an audience: up to that word the psalm lists what was done for other people in other centuries, and from there the deliverance is the singer's own, with no event named, so that any generation can put its own low state into the gap.

In kabbalistic accounts loyalty is the first of the outflowing attributes, the one that gives before anything has been weighed or judged, so a psalm that names it twenty six times is read as a channel held open rather than a receipt for past favours. Notice that the refrain never varies: all the variation sits on the human side of the line, while the answer stays identical, which is itself the claim being made about the giver. The closing title at {{26.1}}, the God of heaven, is the name that dominates the latest books of the Bible, and the reading takes the whole psalm as one long movement from the heavens made with understanding at {{5.2}} down as far as bread, and then back up.
